title: Introduction to the Document Object Model (DOM)
summary: Explains what the DOM is (the browser's tree of objects built from the HTML), how to walk it from the console with firstElementChild / lastElementChild, and how objects have properties (get/set) and methods (called with parentheses). Ends with a challenge to change the third list item's text from the console.

concepts.heading: Why the DOM exists
points: Pages written only in HTML and CSS are static: changes need an edit and a reload by the developer.
Interactivity (reacting to a click, say) must happen live in the visitor's browser, so the page's elements need to be available to code as things to select and change.
The DOM is the browser's catalogue of the page as individual objects. The browser builds it when it loads the HTML, turning each element and its data into a tree of objects.

concepts.heading: The tree structure
points: Everything lives inside a top-level object called document. Under it is the html object, whose children are head and body.
Terminology like a family or org chart: head is a descendant of html; head and body are siblings, not descendants of each other.

Demo page: h1, a checkbox input, a button (Click Me), an unordered list with three li items (the first contains a Google link) and the script element. A tree-visualiser browser extension can draw the DOM for any page.
Body therefore has five element children: h1, input, button, ul, script.

concepts.heading: Walking the tree in the console
points: Typing document in the console prints the whole parsed page and can be expanded.
document.firstElementChild is the html element; document.firstElementChild.firstElementChild is head; .lastElementChild instead gives body.
Going one level deeper from body with firstElementChild reaches the h1. Chain these properties to dig down.
Store the element in a variable (var heading = ...) to reuse it.

concepts.heading: Manipulating a selected element
points: heading.innerHTML = 'Good Bye' replaces the content between the tags, and the page updates immediately.
heading.style.color = 'red' sets an inline style property.
document.querySelector('input') finds the first element matching a CSS selector; calling .click() on the checkbox simulates a click and ticks it.

concepts.heading: Properties vs methods (objects)
points: Objects have properties (describe the object) and methods (things it can do). Car analogy: colour/seats/doors vs drive()/brake()/park().
Dot notation reaches both. car.color reads a property (a getter). car.numberOfDoors = 0 assigns (a setter): the difference is only the equals sign.
car.drive() calls a method; methods always carry parentheses, which may take arguments. That is how you tell them apart from properties.
A method is a function that belongs to an object; a plain function is not attached to one.
DOM element properties mentioned: innerHTML, style, firstChild. Methods mentioned: click(), appendChild() to add a child, setAttribute() to change e.g. href.
The concepts are revisited later, so partial understanding is fine for now.

code_examples.caption: Console exploration
code_examples.code:
document;                                  // whole parsed page
document.firstElementChild;                // <html>
document.firstElementChild.firstElementChild; // <head>
document.firstElementChild.lastElementChild;  // <body>

var heading = document.firstElementChild.lastElementChild.firstElementChild; // the h1
heading.innerHTML = "Good Bye";
heading.style.color = "red";

document.querySelector("input").click();   // ticks the checkbox

code_examples.caption: Properties and methods on a made-up car object
code_examples.code:
car.color;              // get a property
car.numberOfDoors = 0;  // set a property
car.drive();            // call a method

code_examples.caption: Reference-repo script for this lesson
code_examples.code:
document.querySelector("input").click();
document.querySelector("ul").lastElementChild.innerHTML = "I changed the text with javascript";

task.name: Change the third list item from the console
task.starting_point: Downloaded lesson files (index.html, index.js, styles.css) with a ul of three li items; third reads 'Third'.
task.goal: Replace the third li's text with your own name using only the browser console; do not edit the HTML file.
steps: Open the page in Chrome and open DevTools console.
Navigate or select to the third li (walk the tree from document, or use querySelector('ul')).
Take the last child element of the ul.
Set its innerHTML to a new string.
Check the page updates and the HTML file is unchanged.
task.expected_result: The page's last list item shows the new text after pressing Enter in the console.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 16 - The Document Object Model (DOM)/16.02 - Introduction to the Document Object Model (DOM)/script.js

pitfalls: Forgetting that script is also a child of body, so body.lastElementChild is the script, not the ul.
Writing a method without parentheses (nothing is called) or a property with parentheses (not a function).
Using == assignment vs reading: forgetting = turns a setter into a getter.
The console changes are lost on refresh; they do not alter the files.
Reference repo adds a student footer (ignore) and its script is a solution to the challenge, run on page load rather than in the console.

playground.coverage: No playground lesson yet (section 16 has no playground file).
gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Meet the DOM': blurb about HTML becoming a live tree of objects.
Tasks: walk from document to the h1 with firstElementChild/lastElementChild; change its innerHTML and style.color; click() a checkbox; change the third li.
Starter: the demo page (h1, checkbox, button, ul of three li).
Interactive demo: a live DOM-tree view beside the page that highlights the node whose property you edit; also a getter/setter/method cheat card.
